hero.headline: Indian River County schools to offer free meals at six campuses starting this school year
hero.body:
The School District of Indian River County announced Tuesday that students at six schools will have access to free meals during the 2026-2027 school year. The district is utilizing federal nutrition programs, specifically the National School Lunch Program and School Breakfast Program, to eliminate meal costs for eligible students and help families manage daily expenses.

Fellsmere Academy will be the most comprehensive of the participating schools, offering free breakfast and lunch to all students throughout the entire school year. Five other campuses will provide free breakfast at no cost to their student bodies. These schools include Pelican Island Classical Magnet, Citrus Elementary, Dodgertown Elementary, Vero Beach Elementary, and Indian River Academy. Students at these five schools will still need to pay for lunch unless they qualify for additional assistance programs.

Families whose students do not attend one of these six schools may still qualify for free or reduced-price meals based on their household size and income. The district is sending application letters to all homes with parents or guardians in the school district. Interested families can complete an online meal application and submit it to their child's school to determine eligibility for assistance programs based on financial need.

For more information about the meal programs, families can reach out to Shawn O'Keefe, the district's nutrition services director. O'Keefe can be contacted at (772) 564-5041 or shawn.okeefe@indianriverschools.org. The School District of Indian River County offices are located at 6055 62nd Ave in Vero Beach for those who prefer to apply in person or need additional assistance with the application process.

cards.headline: Supreme Court upholds state laws banning transgender girls and women from school sports teams
cards.body:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday upheld state laws barring transgender girls and women from playing on school athletic teams, in another setback for transgender people. The court's conservative majority ruled that state bans in Idaho and West Virginia don't violate the Constitution or the federal law known as Title IX, which prohibits sex discrimination in education. More than two dozen other Republican-led states have adopted bans on female transgender athletes, and the decision extends to them as well.

Becky Pepper-Jackson, a 16-year-old high school sophomore in Bridgeport, West Virginia, has been taking puberty-blocking medication, has publicly identified as a girl since age 8 and has been issued a West Virginia birth certificate recognizing her as female. She is the only transgender person who has sought to compete in girls sports in West Virginia. Pepper-Jackson has progressed from a back-of-the-pack cross-country runner in middle school to statewide champion in the shot put. She beat the second-place finisher by two feet in last month's West Virginia championship meet. In the Idaho case, Lindsay Hecox sued over the state's first-in-the-nation ban for the chance to try out for the women's track and cross-country teams at Boise State University in Idaho. She didn't make either squad because she was too slow, her lawyer Kathleen Hartnett told the court during arguments in January, but she competed in club-level soccer and running.

Idaho's law, state Solicitor General Alan Hurst said, is necessary for fair competition because, where sports are concerned, men and women are obviously not the same. Lawyers for Pepper-Jackson argued that such distinctions generally make sense but that their client has none of those advantages because of the unique circumstances of her early transition. NCAA president Charlie Baker told Congress in 2024 that he was aware of only 10 transgender athletes out of more than half a million students on college teams. Despite the small numbers, the issue has taken on outsize importance. Olympic and Paralympic Committees banned transgender women from women's sports after President Donald Trump, a Republican, signed an executive order aimed at barring their participation.

An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll conducted in October 2025 found that about 6 in 10 U.S. adults strongly or somewhat favored requiring transgender children and teenagers to compete only on sports teams that match the sex they were assigned at birth, not the gender they identify with, while about 2 in 10 were strongly or somewhat opposed and about one-quarter did not have an opinion. About 2.1 million adults, or 0.8%, and 724,000 people ages 13 to 17, or 3.3%, identify as transgender in the U.S., according to the Williams Institute at the UCLA School of Law.

cards.headline: Supreme Court upholds birthright citizenship, rejecting Trump limits on children of undocumented immigrants
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court on Tuesday upheld a broad conception of birthright citizenship, rejecting President Donald Trump's executive order that would have denied citizenship to children born to people who are in the United States illegally or temporarily.
cards.body:
The justices relied on a long-settled understanding of the 14th Amendment, adopted after the Civil War, and more recent federal laws in ruling that anyone born in the country, with very limited exceptions, is a citizen. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the court that citizenship was the right to have rights and that the Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to every free-born person in this land. Three conservative justices would have allowed the restrictions to take effect.

The Republican president's restrictions had been blocked by several lower courts and had not taken effect anywhere in the U.S. During arguments in April, both conservative and liberal justices questioned the order's legality in a momentous case that was magnified by Trump's unprecedented attendance in the courtroom. Trump's order would have upended widely held views that the 14th Amendment confers citizenship on everyone born in the U.S., excluding only the children of foreign diplomats and those born to a foreign occupying force. The amendment was intended to ensure that Black people, including former slaves, had citizenship, though the Citizenship Clause is written more broadly.

More than one-quarter of a million babies born in the U.S. each year would have been affected by the executive order, according to research by the Migration Policy Institute and Pennsylvania State University's Population Research Institute. While Trump has largely focused on illegal immigration in his rhetoric and actions, the birthright citizenship restrictions also would have applied to people who are legally in the United States, including students and applicants for green cards, or permanent resident status.

cards.headline: Fatal crash on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County kills 2, fifth traffic death in four days
cards.teaser: A crash on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County killed two people Monday afternoon and closed all lanes in both directions for multiple hours, causing heavy dela.
cards.body:
A crash on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County killed two people Monday afternoon and closed all lanes in both directions for multiple hours, causing heavy delays. According to the Martin County Fire Rescue, the wreck happened near mile marker 132 at about 3 p.m. In addition to the two fatalities, firefighter-paramedics transported one person with traumatic injuries by ground to the hospital. The Martin County Sheriff's Office shut down both northbound and southbound lanes of the Turnpike completely at 3:49 p.m. All lanes reopened at about 8 p.m. The cause of the crash has not been released.

According to the sheriff's office, this is the fifth traffic fatality in four days in Martin County. A Palm City man died overnight following a two-vehicle crash on the Turnpike early Monday morning. Additionally, two people were killed in a head-on crash Saturday morning on Allapattah Road in Indiantown.

cards.headline: Florida becomes first state to fund statewide Jewish student safety program after pilot shows reduced harassment
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a roughly $2.3 million investment expanding the Florida Hillel Jewish Student Safety Initiative to seven campuses across the state, reaching an estimated 25,000-plus Jewish students.
cards.body:
The Florida Hillel Jewish Student Safety Initiative began last year as a three-campus pilot at the University of Florida, Florida State and the University of South Florida. It paired security personnel, surveillance and hardening with antisemitism education, stronger ties to university leadership and faster incident response. After a single year, Florida's Jewish students were reporting harassment at roughly half the national rate. Now the program goes statewide, adding Florida International University, Florida Atlantic University, the University of Central Florida and the University of Miami.

Sen. Alexis Calatayud, a Miami Republican, and Rep. Allison Tant, a Tallahassee Democrat, championed the legislation. Sen. Lawrence McClure protected the line in a lean budget year. Rabbi Jordan Gerson, Executive Director of Central Florida Hillel at UCF, said Florida has demonstrated that it is committed to fostering an environment where every student can proudly and openly embrace their identity. Brian Pelc, Executive Director of Hillel at FSU, said the expansion will allow the program to improve safety, combat campus antisemitism and tackle specific issues brought to light in the 2025 Jewish Student Life Survey.

Jon Warech, Executive Director of Hillel at FIU, said the program arrives at exactly the moment it is needed, so that no student has to choose between their education and their identity. Karen Cyphers, partner at Sachs Media and president of the Tallahassee Jewish Federation, said the promising data from this pilot program gives reason for hope at a time when most trendlines are deeply concerning.

cards.headline: Supreme Court strikes down federal limits on political party spending in coordination with candidates
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court on Tuesday erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, striking down a federal election law that is more than 50 years old.
cards.body:
Prodded by a Republican-led lawsuit that includes Vice President JD Vance, the court's conservative justices were again in the majority of the latest decision that upended congressionally enacted limits on raising and spending money to influence elections. The limits on party spending stem from a desire to prevent large donors from skirting caps on individual contributions to a candidate by directing unlimited sums to the party, with the understanding that the money will be spent on behalf of the candidate. The Supreme Court had previously upheld the limits in 2001.

The Republican committees for House and Senate candidates filed the lawsuit in Ohio in 2022, joined by Vance, then a senator from Ohio, and then-Rep. Byron Donalds. After President Donald Trump took office for his second term, the Federal Election Commission dropped its defense of the law and joined with Republicans in urging that it be overturned. Democrats had called on the court to uphold the law, even though there is wide agreement that the spending limits have hurt political parties in an era of unlimited spending by other organizations. Last year, the coordinated party spending for Senate races ranged from $127,200 in several states with small populations to nearly $4 million in California, the most populous state. For House races, the limits were $127,200 in states with only one representative and $63,600 everywhere else.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County secures $30 million in state budget including Tri-Rail lifeline
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County secured over $30 million in the new Florida state budget, including $60 million to keep Tri-Rail operating and funding for major infrastructure projects.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County secured over $30 million in the new Florida state budget, representing 75% of the funding requested by local agencies and organizations. The overall $117 billion state budget includes major local wins, especially for transportation, though Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed nearly $1.6 billion in proposed spending statewide. Tri-Rail received the $60 million it needed to keep operating after facing a potential July shutdown without state help. Florida State Senator Mack Bernard called the funding a lifeline for commuters traveling between Palm Beach County, Broward and Dade counties. The county also secured $1.5 million for the new Riviera Beach water treatment plant, $2 million for drainage repairs to Australian Avenue from 45th Street to Palm Beach Lakes, and $3 million for traffic safety improvements on Okeechobee Boulevard.

Other approved funding includes $1.5 million for a special needs shelter at Arc of the Palm Beaches in West Palm Beach and $1.5 million for the Teen Readiness Center at the Boys & Girls Club. However, several Palm Beach County priorities were vetoed, including $2 million for water treatment plant expansions, $900,000 for road improvements and beautification in South Bay, $125,000 for Ocean Inlet beach access improvements, and $200,000 for repairs and operations at Delray Beach's historic American Legion building. State Representative Rob Long said he plans to push again for the American Legion funding during next year's budget cycle.

cards.headline: Singer Island Gateway development proposal raises concerns over Blue Heron Bridge reef
cards.teaser: A proposed 25-story waterfront development near Phil Foster Park on Singer Island is raising questions about impacts to a world-renowned reef that draws divers from across the globe.
cards.body:
A New York-based developer, The Continuum Company, has proposed Singer Island Gateway, an approximately $14 million mixed-use project along 2525 Lake Drive in Palm Beach County. The plan includes hundreds of residential units, commercial and public space, and a marina near the base of Blue Heron Bridge, rising 25 stories at the entrance to Singer Island.

Beneath the shallow waters surrounding Phil Foster Park at the base of Blue Heron Bridge lies an underwater ecosystem that draws divers and snorkelers from across the globe. Gary Heiser, who grew up in the area, said the scale and placement of the project are fundamentally incompatible with the location. He worries that construction activity, increased shade from the tower, and the addition of a marina could disrupt the marine life that has made the reef world-renowned. An environmental study published on the developer's website concluded the planned development would have no impact on the marine life in the Lake Worth Lagoon, stating the ecosystem will remain unchanged. However, Heiser expressed skepticism, saying he would like to see more research. Nothing has been approved yet. Residents have started a petition against the proposal, and the developer has been contacted for comment.

cards.headline: One person dies in Hobe Sound house fire, State Fire Marshal investigating
cards.teaser: One person died Monday afternoon in a house fire in the 7000 block of Southeast Cactus Trail in Hobe Sound.
cards.body:
One person died Monday afternoon in a house fire in Hobe Sound. Martin County Fire Rescue responded just after 3 p.m. to a home in the 7000 block of Southeast Cactus Trail. When crews from Martin County Fire Rescue Station 32 arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from all doors and windows of the home. Firefighters entered the house, located an unresponsive person, and removed them from the home.

Paramedics treated the victim and transported them by ambulance to a hospital with life-threatening injuries. Martin County Fire Rescue later confirmed the person died. Stuart Fire Rescue also responded to assist under a mutual aid agreement. The State Fire Marshal has been notified and is investigating the cause of the fire.

cards.headline: Two killed in Florida's Turnpike crash in Martin County, fifth traffic fatality in four days
cards.teaser: A crash that killed two people on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County near mile marker 132 closed all lanes in both directions for multiple hours Monday afternoon.
cards.body:
A crash that killed two people on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County closed all lanes in both directions for multiple hours on Monday afternoon, causing heavy delays. According to the Martin County Fire Rescue Facebook page, the wreck happened near mile marker 132 at about 3 p.m. In addition to the two people killed, firefighter-paramedics took one person with traumatic injuries by ground to the hospital. The Martin County Sheriff's Office posted at 3:49 p.m. that both northbound and southbound lanes of the Turnpike were completely shut down. All lanes reopened at about 8 p.m. The cause of the crash has not been released.

According to the sheriff's office, this is the fifth traffic fatality in four days in Martin County. A Palm City man died overnight after a two-vehicle crash on the Turnpike early Monday morning. Two people were also killed in a head-on crash Saturday morning on Allapattah Road in Indiantown.

cards.headline: Two Palm Beach County women arrested in Lake Worth Beach human trafficking operation
cards.teaser: Diana Chaparro Contreras and Sandra Peralta Aguilar are accused of running a human trafficking operation out of a Lake Worth Beach home where a California woman was allegedly forced into prostitution.
cards.body:
Diana Chaparro Contreras, 33, and Sandra Peralta Aguilar, 50, are each facing several charges, including human trafficking and profiting from or arranging prostitution. Both are now in the Palm Beach County Jail. The case began in January when a California victim applied for housekeeping jobs on Indeed and was offered $35 an hour and flown to Florida. When she arrived at the Lake Worth Beach home on S. M Street, her passport, Social Security card, and work permit were taken. She told detectives she was threatened with deportation and was forced into sex with men who came into the home.

The victim reported being kept in a room with boarded windows and was forced to sleep with seven men before escaping by using a lamp to break through plywood boards. She said a possible 15-year-old girl was also present in the brothel. Throughout the months-long investigation, officials found several men coming in and out of the house. In April, investigators learned the brothel had been moved to another location nearly a mile away. Investigators also found Chaparro handled more than $177,000 in cash and bank transactions. Anyone who suspects human trafficking activity is asked to contact the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office or the Human Trafficking Coalition of the Palm Beaches at 561-267-5783.

cards.headline: Central Florida projects and programs hit by state budget vetoes
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed nearly $1.6 billion in proposed spending from the state budget, affecting projects and programs in Central Florida.
cards.body:
The overall $117 billion Florida state budget for 2026-2027 was finalized with nearly $1.6 billion in proposed spending vetoed by Governor Ron DeSantis.

The budget vetoes came as part of a statewide reduction in spending proposals submitted by local agencies and organizations. Communities across Florida have been reviewing the finalized budget to determine which projects received funding and which were eliminated through the governor's veto pen.

hero.headline: Two Palm Beach County women arrested, accused of human trafficking operation in Lake Worth Beach
hero.teaser: Diana Chaparro Contreras, 33, and Sandra Peralta Aguilar, 50, are accused of running a human trafficking operation where a California woman was allegedly lured with a fake job offer and forced into prostitution.
hero.body:
Diana Chaparro Contreras, 33, and Sandra Peralta Aguilar, 50, are facing multiple charges including human trafficking and profiting from or arranging prostitution. Both women are currently held in the Palm Beach County Jail. Authorities say they operated a trafficking scheme out of a Lake Worth Beach residence where a California woman was recruited under false pretenses and forced into sexual exploitation.

The investigation began in January when the victim responded to a housekeeping job posting on Indeed and was offered $35 per hour. After accepting the position, she was flown to Florida and brought to a home on S. M Street in Lake Worth Beach. Upon arrival, her passport, Social Security card, and work permit were confiscated. The victim reported being threatened with deportation and coerced into sexual acts with men who visited the residence. She was confined to a room with boarded windows and allegedly forced to engage in sexual activity with seven men before managing to escape. The victim used a lamp to break through the plywood covering the windows. She also reported that a possible 15-year-old girl was present at the location.

Law enforcement tracked the operation over several months, observing multiple men entering and leaving the property. In April, authorities discovered the operation had relocated to another address approximately one mile away. Financial records revealed that Chaparro handled more than $177,000 in cash and bank transactions associated with the trafficking scheme.

Laura Cusack, an advocate with the Human Trafficking Coalition of the Palm Beaches, emphasized that such operations can occur anywhere in the community. "It doesn't just happen in a vacuum or in the underground world. It could happen in the house next door," Cusack said. She stressed that community awareness serves as one of the most effective tools for identifying trafficking activity. Cusack noted that neighbors and community members who recognize suspicious patterns, such as unusually high foot traffic, can make a critical difference in stopping exploitation. "These predators are in our community. They can target our children so it just takes one person to make the call, report what they see and that can make all the difference," Cusack said. Anyone who suspects human trafficking is encouraged to contact the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office or reach out to the Human Trafficking Coalition of the Palm Beaches at 561-267-5783 or htcoalitionpb@gmail.com.

cards.headline: Palm City man dies in early morning crash involving SUV and semi-truck on Florida's Turnpike

cards.headline: Fort Pierce diver Greer Boyd found dead near Fort Pierce Inlet after diving for lost trolling motor
cards.teaser: A 63-year-old Fort Pierce man died Friday while attempting to recover a trolling motor that fell overboard near the Fort Pierce Inlet.
cards.body:
Lucie County Sheriff's Office has identified the diver found dead Friday near the Fort Pierce Inlet as Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce. According to investigators, Boyd was fishing with friends earlier in the day when the boat's trolling motor became detached and went overboard. The group returned to the area with diving equipment to attempt recovery of the motor. Boyd entered the water alone, and only his buoyancy compensator and air tank were located approximately 40 yards from the boat.

Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday regarding a missing diver. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed four vessels to assist in the search. Martin County Fire Rescue Lt. Daniel DeGrazia, who was off-duty at the time, was able to assist in the operation. DeGrazia recovered Boyd's body at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. An autopsy is scheduled for today.

cards.headline: 400-pound black bear killed after being struck by car on Southwest Martin Highway
cards.teaser: A 400-pound male black bear died Monday morning after being hit by a car on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard in Martin County.
cards.body:
A 400-pound male black bear was killed Monday morning after being struck by a car on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard. The driver was not speeding and stopped to wait for Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies to arrive. According to the driver's account to deputies, the bear ran into the roadway before being struck by the vehicle. The driver was not injured, but the bear died at the scene. Major Ruben Romero with the sheriff's office emphasized the importance of driver awareness regarding wildlife, particularly on rural roads during morning and evening hours.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission removed the bear from the scene. Michael Orlando, bear program coordinator with FWC, believes the bear was in the middle of dispersing, when bears leave their mother and pack to find a new home. According to Orlando, bears can walk 50 to 100 miles in any direction during this period. The bear is currently with FWC in Collier County, where officials will collect data to determine its origin. This marks the second bear sighting on the Treasure Coast this month.

hero.headline: Singer Island development proposal raises concerns over world-renowned Blue Heron Bridge reef
hero.teaser: A New York developer has proposed Singer Island Gateway, a 25-story mixed-use project along 2525 Lake Drive that would include a marina near the base of Blue Heron Bridge.
hero.body:
The Continuum Company, a New York-based developer, has proposed Singer Island Gateway, a mixed-use project valued at approximately $14 million at 2525 Lake Drive. The development would feature hundreds of residential units, commercial and public space, and a marina near the base of Blue Heron Bridge at the entrance to Singer Island in Palm Beach County. The main structure would rise 25 stories above the waterfront location.

The project has drawn attention because it would be situated above Phil Foster Park, an underwater ecosystem that attracts divers and snorkelers from around the world. Visitors to the area describe the marine environment in glowing terms. "A few stingrays, some like rainbow fish," one visitor noted. Another described "blue and yellow fish, and some pink coral," while a third mentioned seeing "yellow coral, which I've never seen before, and striped fish." One diver called it simply "beautiful, amazing." The reef's global reputation stems from the unique combination of marine life found in these shallow waters beneath the bridge.

Longtime resident Gary Heiser, who grew up in the area, opposes the development based on both its scale and potential environmental impact. He believes the 25-story tower is inappropriate for the location, saying "It's way too drastic for this location. Twenty-five stories would be okay in Chicago, but it doesn't work right here." Beyond aesthetic concerns, Heiser worries that construction activity, shade from the tall building, and the marina could harm the marine ecosystem. He expressed skepticism about the developer's environmental conclusions, stating "I find it hard to believe that there'd be no impact. I would like to see more research."

The developer has published an environmental study on its website in which a geoscientist concluded the project would have no impact on marine life in the Lake Worth Lagoon, with the ecosystem remaining unchanged. Not all area visitors share Heiser's concerns. One diver indicated his position would depend on whether the project actually threatens the reef, saying "If it doesn't disturb the reef, I don't see a problem with it."

The project has not yet received approval. The developer was contacted for additional comment, with a response pending. Meanwhile, residents have organized a petition against the proposal.

For questions about the meal programs, families can contact Shawn O'Keefe, the district's nutrition services director, at (772) 564-5041 or shawn.okeefe@indianriverschools.org. The School District of Indian River County offices are located at 6055 62nd Ave in Vero Beach.

cards.headline: 400-pound black bear killed after being hit on Southwest Martin Highway
cards.teaser: A 400-pound male black bear died Monday morning after getting hit by a car on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard.
cards.body:
A 400-pound male black bear was killed Monday morning after being hit by a car on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard. Major Ruben Romero with the Martin County Sheriff's Office said the driver was not speeding and stopped to wait for deputies to arrive. According to the driver's account to deputies, the bear ran into the roadway before being struck by the vehicle. The driver was not injured, but the bear died at the scene. Romero stressed the importance of driver awareness regarding wildlife, particularly on rural roads during morning and evening hours.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission removed the bear from the scene. Michael Orlando, bear program coordinator with FWC, said he believes the bear was in the middle of dispersing, when bears get old enough to leave their mother and pack to find a new home. Orlando explained that bears walk 50 to 100 miles in any direction while trying to figure out where they are going. The bear is currently with FWC in Collier County, where officials will collect data to determine where it came from. This is the second bear sighting on the Treasure Coast this month.

hero.headline: Six Indian River County schools to offer free meals for students
hero.teaser: Fellsmere Academy and five other schools will provide free breakfast or lunch through federal nutrition programs during the 2026-2027 school year.
hero.body:
Students attending six Indian River County schools will have access to free meals during the 2026-2027 school year through federally funded nutrition programs. The School District of Indian River County announced Tuesday that it will participate in the National School Lunch Program and School Breakfast Program to provide no-cost meals to eligible students, helping families reduce daily food expenses.

Fellsmere Academy will be the most comprehensive participant in the program, offering free breakfast and lunch to all students throughout the entire school year. Five other schools in the district will provide free breakfast to their students: Pelican Island Classical Magnet, Citrus Elementary, Dodgertown Elementary, Vero Beach Elementary, and Indian River Academy. These six schools represent a significant expansion of meal support across the county's education system.

Beyond the schools offering universal free meals, other families in the Indian River County school district may still qualify for free or reduced-price meals based on their household size and income. The district is sending application letters to all homes in the district to inform parents and guardians about the program. Families who wish to apply can complete an online meal application and submit it to their child's school. This process allows the district to determine eligibility for families who do not automatically receive free meals.

Parents and guardians with questions about the meal programs can reach out to Shawn O'Keefe, the district's nutrition services director, at (772) 564-5041 or shawn.okeefe@indianriverschools.org. The School District of Indian River County main offices are located at 6055 62nd Ave in Vero Beach for those seeking additional information or assistance.

cards.headline: One person dies in Hobe Sound house fire on Southeast Cactus Trail
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue responded to heavy smoke at a home in the 7000 block of Southeast Cactus Trail Monday afternoon, where one person was found unresponsive and later died.
cards.body:
One person died Monday afternoon in a house fire in Hobe Sound, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Firefighters responded just after 3 p.m. to a home in the 7000 block of Southeast Cactus Trail. When crews from Martin County Fire Rescue Station 32 arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from all doors and windows of the home. Firefighters entered the house, located an unresponsive person, and removed them from the home.

Paramedics treated the victim and transported them by ambulance to a hospital with life-threatening injuries. Martin County Fire Rescue later confirmed the person died. Stuart Fire Rescue also responded to assist under a mutual aid agreement. The State Fire Marshal has been notified and is investigating the cause of the fire.

cards.headline: Woman, 78, killed after SUV rolls backward in Port St. Lucie driveway
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie woman died Sunday morning when an SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.
cards.body:
A 78-year-old woman was killed Sunday morning after an SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The incident happened at approximately 10:47 a.m. when a 2016 Lincoln MKX SUV was parked in a residential driveway. The woman was standing outside the vehicle near the open driver's door when the SUV began rolling backward. The open door struck her, knocking her to the ground. Her adult son, 59, was in the passenger seat and had started the vehicle. The cause of the rollback remains under investigation.

The woman was rushed to Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she was pronounced deceased at 11:19 a.m. Neighbors who knew the woman for several years spoke about her kindness. "I saw the ambulance, the fire trucks, and two or three police cars. I felt sad, sad because I've known her for many years," said neighbor Daisy Cardona. "On Sundays, they would bring us bread, cupcakes, donuts, and sometimes cakes. May she rest in peace and my condolences to her family.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets game postponed, rescheduled for late July in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: The St.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets game against the Mussels has been postponed and will be rescheduled for late July in Port St. Lucie, according to MLB.com.

The announcement was made Saturday regarding the game postponement. The rescheduled date will take place later in July at the Mets home stadium in Port St. Lucie.

The St. Lucie Mets are the Class A affiliate of the New York Mets and play their home games in Port St. Lucie. The team competes in the Florida State League.

Fans who purchased tickets for the original game date should check with the St. Lucie Mets organization for information about the rescheduled game in late July.

hero.headline: Boca Raton City Hall hosts Independence Day market July 4 with free admission
hero.teaser: The SoFlo Market will transform Boca Raton City Hall into a Fourth of July celebration featuring a kids parade, DJ, vendors, and food with free admission.
hero.body:
The SoFlo Market will host a Fourth of July celebration at Boca Raton City Hall on Saturday, July 4, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. with free admission. Founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas said the monthly market will add patriotic flair to the Independence Day edition. The first 20 children through the gate will receive a free gift.

Family entertainment includes face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf, and balloon twisting alongside handmade crafts and desserts. The market's flamboyant flamingo mascot will make a live appearance. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to attend.

Kyle, Freitas' son, and Eddie, her husband, are part of the organizing team. Electricity will be powered by generators on site. The event takes place at 201 West Palmetto Park Road and will be featured on the market's Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and YouTube channels throughout the day.

cards.headline: MusicWorks in Vero Beach launches fourteenth concert season to expand cultural tourism
cards.teaser: MusicWorks in Vero Beach has launched its fourteenth concert season, positioning Florida alongside California, Texas, New York, Tennessee, Georgia, Illinois, Ne.
cards.body:
MusicWorks in Vero Beach has launched its fourteenth concert season, positioning Florida alongside California, Texas, New York, Tennessee, Georgia, Illinois, Nevada, Arizona, Michigan and Massachusetts in expanding cultural tourism and inspiring multi-state travel. The concert series represents a significant expansion of cultural offerings in Indian River County.

The season launch places Vero Beach on a multi-state cultural tourism map, aligning the city with major markets across the country. The concert series aims to draw visitors from multiple states to the Treasure Coast for cultural events.

MusicWorks has been presenting concerts in Vero Beach for fourteen seasons, building a reputation that now attracts national attention. The organization's expansion into broader cultural tourism markets represents a milestone for the Indian River County arts community.

The concert season will bring performances to Vero Beach throughout the coming months, offering residents and visitors access to professional concerts in the local market. The organization positions itself as part of a network of cultural destinations spanning ten states plus Florida.

cards.headline: George Snow Scholarship Fund in Boca Raton awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton nonprofit awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County, according to President Tim Snow. The program offers four-year commitments designed to bridge the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford.

GSSF's services extend beyond financial assistance. Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted the organization provides mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast. The Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, offers professional, formal, and casual wear along with footwear and accessories through new or gently used donations. One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University.

hero.headline: Supreme Court upholds state laws banning transgender girls and women from school sports teams
hero.body:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday upheld state laws barring transgender girls and women from playing on school athletic teams, in another setback for transgender people. The court's conservative majority ruled that state bans in Idaho and West Virginia don't violate the Constitution or the federal law known as Title IX, which prohibits sex discrimination in education. More than two dozen other Republican-led states have adopted bans on female transgender athletes, and the decision extends to them as well.

Becky Pepper-Jackson, a 16-year-old high school sophomore in Bridgeport, West Virginia, has been taking puberty-blocking medication, has publicly identified as a girl since age 8 and has been issued a West Virginia birth certificate recognizing her as female. She is the only transgender person who has sought to compete in girls sports in West Virginia. Pepper-Jackson has progressed from a back-of-the-pack cross-country runner in middle school to statewide champion in the shot put. She beat the second-place finisher by two feet in last month's West Virginia championship meet. In the Idaho case, Lindsay Hecox sued over the state's first-in-the-nation ban for the chance to try out for the women's track and cross-country teams at Boise State University in Idaho. She didn't make either squad because she was too slow, her lawyer Kathleen Hartnett told the court during arguments in January, but she competed in club-level soccer and running.

Idaho's law, state Solicitor General Alan Hurst said, is necessary for fair competition because, where sports are concerned, men and women are obviously not the same. Lawyers for Pepper-Jackson argued that such distinctions generally make sense but that their client has none of those advantages because of the unique circumstances of her early transition. NCAA president Charlie Baker told Congress in 2024 that he was aware of only 10 transgender athletes out of more than half a million students on college teams. Despite the small numbers, the issue has taken on outsize importance. Olympic and Paralympic Committees banned transgender women from women's sports after President Donald Trump, a Republican, signed an executive order aimed at barring their participation.

An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll conducted in October 2025 found that about 6 in 10 U.S. adults strongly or somewhat favored requiring transgender children and teenagers to compete only on sports teams that match the sex they were assigned at birth, not the gender they identify with, while about 2 in 10 were strongly or somewhat opposed and about one-quarter did not have an opinion. About 2.1 million adults, or 0.8%, and 724,000 people ages 13 to 17, or 3.3%, identify as transgender in the U.S., according to the Williams Institute at the UCLA School of Law.

cards.headline: Supreme Court upholds birthright citizenship, rejecting Trump limits on children of undocumented immigrants
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court on Tuesday upheld a broad conception of birthright citizenship, rejecting President Donald Trump's executive order that would have denied citizenship to children born to people who are in the United States illegally or temporarily.
cards.body:
The justices relied on a long-settled understanding of the 14th Amendment, adopted after the Civil War, and more recent federal laws in ruling that anyone born in the country, with very limited exceptions, is a citizen. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the court that citizenship was the right to have rights and that the Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to every free-born person in this land. Three conservative justices would have allowed the restrictions to take effect.

The Republican president's restrictions had been blocked by several lower courts and had not taken effect anywhere in the U.S. During arguments in April, both conservative and liberal justices questioned the order's legality in a momentous case that was magnified by Trump's unprecedented attendance in the courtroom. Trump's order would have upended widely held views that the 14th Amendment confers citizenship on everyone born in the U.S., excluding only the children of foreign diplomats and those born to a foreign occupying force. The amendment was intended to ensure that Black people, including former slaves, had citizenship, though the Citizenship Clause is written more broadly.

More than one-quarter of a million babies born in the U.S. each year would have been affected by the executive order, according to research by the Migration Policy Institute and Pennsylvania State University's Population Research Institute. While Trump has largely focused on illegal immigration in his rhetoric and actions, the birthright citizenship restrictions also would have applied to people who are legally in the United States, including students and applicants for green cards, or permanent resident status.

cards.headline: Florida becomes first state to fund statewide Jewish student safety program after pilot shows reduced harassment
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a roughly $2.3 million investment expanding the Florida Hillel Jewish Student Safety Initiative to seven campuses across the state, reaching an estimated 25,000-plus Jewish students.
cards.body:
The Florida Hillel Jewish Student Safety Initiative began last year as a three-campus pilot at the University of Florida, Florida State and the University of South Florida. It paired security personnel, surveillance and hardening with antisemitism education, stronger ties to university leadership and faster incident response. After a single year, Florida's Jewish students were reporting harassment at roughly half the national rate. Now the program goes statewide, adding Florida International University, Florida Atlantic University, the University of Central Florida and the University of Miami.

Sen. Alexis Calatayud, a Miami Republican, and Rep. Allison Tant, a Tallahassee Democrat, championed the legislation. Sen. Lawrence McClure protected the line in a lean budget year. Rabbi Jordan Gerson, Executive Director of Central Florida Hillel at UCF, said Florida has demonstrated that it is committed to fostering an environment where every student can proudly and openly embrace their identity. Brian Pelc, Executive Director of Hillel at FSU, said the expansion will allow the program to improve safety, combat campus antisemitism and tackle specific issues brought to light in the 2025 Jewish Student Life Survey.

Jon Warech, Executive Director of Hillel at FIU, said the program arrives at exactly the moment it is needed, so that no student has to choose between their education and their identity. Karen Cyphers, partner at Sachs Media and president of the Tallahassee Jewish Federation, said the promising data from this pilot program gives reason for hope at a time when most trendlines are deeply concerning.

cards.headline: DeSantis cuts $2.2 million for low-income senior services in South Florida despite statewide increases
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed more than $2.2 million in funding for senior centers, meals-on-wheels programs and other services for low-income elderly residents in South Florida, part of $95 million in local South Florida project cuts.
cards.body:
Of more than $95 million DeSantis slashed from local South Florida projects this week, part of $1.6 billion in total vetoes in the coming $117.6 billion state budget, more than $2.2 million will affect the area's low-income seniors. The cuts went both right and left, with about as many Republican sponsors of the projects as Democrats. Miami-Dade saw twice as many vetoes as Broward, which had twice as many as Palm Beach County. While funding was removed for specific seniors-specific projects in the region, DeSantis increased overall spending on Florida's elderly residents, adding $7.5 million for a total of $131 million to increase services through the Community Care for the Elderly and Home Care for the Elderly programs, and $3 million more for a total of $73.1 million to serve additional seniors through Florida's Alzheimer's Disease Initiative.

The biggest-ticket appropriation to lose funding was a $600,000 set-aside for the construction of a multipurpose, weather-protected outdoor space for economically disadvantaged seniors enrolled in West Miami's hot meals program. Sen. Ileana Garcia and Coral Gables Republican Rep. Demi Busatta filed matching appropriation requests for the shovel-ready project, which received $300,000 from the state last year. DeSantis also vetoed $500,000 meant for the Age Well program, which provides nursing, therapy, social work and physician home visits for low- to moderate-income seniors who are not eligible for long-term care funding. The program is administered by Good Will Enterprises Group Corp., a Coral Gables-based nonprofit that says it serves up to 1,500 seniors.

In Broward, DeSantis cut $448,000 to help fund at-home transition care for elderly residents whose needs aren't covered by long-term care Medicaid, Medicare or other insurance. The Coming Home Senior Hospital Transition Program is administered by Broward-based nonprofit United HomeCare and provides 90-day episodic in-home care, including nursing assessments, case management, personal care services and home-delivered meals. The Governor also nixed $250,000 meant for an expansion of the Senior Activity Center in Pompano Beach.

cards.headline: Supreme Court strikes down federal limits on political party spending in coordination with candidates
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court on Tuesday erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, striking down a federal election law that is more than 50 years old.
cards.body:
Prodded by a Republican-led lawsuit that includes Vice President JD Vance, the court's conservative justices were again in the majority of the latest decision that upended congressionally enacted limits on raising and spending money to influence elections. The limits on party spending stem from a desire to prevent large donors from skirting caps on individual contributions to a candidate by directing unlimited sums to the party, with the understanding that the money will be spent on behalf of the candidate. The Supreme Court had previously upheld the limits in 2001.

The Republican committees for House and Senate candidates filed the lawsuit in Ohio in 2022, joined by Vance, then a senator from Ohio, and then-Rep. Byron Donalds. After President Donald Trump took office for his second term, the Federal Election Commission dropped its defense of the law and joined with Republicans in urging that it be overturned. Democrats had called on the court to uphold the law, even though there is wide agreement that the spending limits have hurt political parties in an era of unlimited spending by other organizations. Last year, the coordinated party spending for Senate races ranged from $127,200 in several states with small populations to nearly $4 million in California, the most populous state. For House races, the limits were $127,200 in states with only one representative and $63,600 everywhere else.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds launches $20 million ad buy for governor race, pledging lower costs and ratepayer protections
cards.teaser: The Friends of Byron Donalds political committee launched two new television and digital ads statewide, part of the committee's $20 million buy, the largest single media investment of the 2026 gubernatorial race.
cards.body:
The spots, Jack Up and Shot, are now live across cable, broadcast television and streaming platforms across Florida. In Jack Up, Donalds makes clear he stands with President Donald Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis on AI data centers, pledging to protect Florida ratepayers from utility rate hikes and negative environmental impacts. In Shot, he speaks directly to the cost-of-living squeeze facing families across the state, opening with his own story: a mother who worked two jobs in Brooklyn and still lived paycheck to paycheck, and his move to Florida nearly 30 years ago that gave him the chance to build something from nothing.

Ryan Smith, Chairman of the Friends of Byron Donalds political committee, said Donalds is laser-focused on making Florida more affordable for families, seniors and young people. These ads tell the story of who Byron is and what he'll fight for as governor: lower costs, consumer protections and keeping Florida the state where everyone can achieve their dreams. The buy reflects Donalds' dominance as he continues to shatter fundraising records, build a ground operation that has knocked more than 175,000 doors and command the most conservative backing in the field, including the endorsements of President Trump, Donald Trump Jr., Elon Musk, Charlie Kirk, U.S. Sen. Rick Scott, the majority of Florida's sheriffs and dozens of legislators and conservative leaders across the state.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Democrat Lois Frankel endorses Leela Gray for Congress in Pinellas County CD 13 race
cards.teaser: U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel, a Palm Beach County Democrat representing Florida's 22nd Congressional District, endorsed Leela Gray for Congress in Florida's 13th Congressional District, citing Gray's military service and working-family background.
cards.body:
Frankel, co-Chair of the House Democratic Women's Caucus, said Gray understands the struggles of working families from a lifetime of hard work, service and sacrifice. As a working mom, veteran and proven leader who served the nation for 30 years in uniform and fought for veterans and economic opportunity, Leela has the grit, experience and heart to deliver for the people of Pinellas County, Frankel said. Gray said she is honored to have Frankel's support, highlighting her work on behalf of families and women in public life.

A lawyer and third-generation veteran, Gray spent more than 30 years in uniform, including two combat deployments and a peacekeeping mission. She retired in 2018 as Deputy Commanding General of U.S. Army Central and later advised U.S. Army Cyber Command on national cyber policy modernization. After retiring from the military, Gray served on nonprofit and private sector advisory boards and earned her law degree with a focus on helping veterans access healthcare and other benefits. She and her husband, Tony, have lived in the Tampa Bay area for more than 20 years. Gray faces fellow Democrats John William Liccione and Brandt Robinson in the Aug. 18 Primary, while incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna is uncontested for the Republican nomination.
